catalog_quote: Reichard 1925:11, §4 ACCENT: "The question of accent in Wiyot is a difficult one. One point is clear, however, namely, that, although stress is of extremely great importance in making the language intelligible, it is not a morphological feature. No rules have been formulated which show where the stress should be placed. Disyllabic words may be stressed on either syllable, and the accent does not remain stable. That is to say, when used independently, a word may be stressed on a certain syllable, but if the same word is found in a sentence the accent may have shifted. The same may be said for polysyllabic words. But should a word have as many as four or five syllables the tendency is toward placing equal stress on the two middle, or approximately middle, syllables. This rule is not by any means absolute. readall_conflicts: The pre-existing disagreement stands as the catalog records it: StressTyp2 codes Wiyot as weight-sensitive (leftmost heavy syllable, else initial, 'tentative') on the basis of Proulx 1984:195, whose 'heavy' is a formerly (Proto-Algic) long vowel, i.e. a historical condition, and who calls the stress 'phonemic underlying'; Reichard 1925 §4 (p.11, read in the original by the catalog) says no placement rules can be formulated and that accent position shifts in connected speech. WALS (14A No fixed stress, 15A Unbounded, 16A Lexical stress, 17A No rhythmic stress, all sourced to Proulx 1984) sides with the lexical reading. Teeter 1964, the best grammar, remains unopened by anyone (lending-only / search-only copies).

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding Reichard 1925 §4 'Accent' passage is verbatim at p.11 of the held archive.org scanned (line 856 ff.), locator correct; the Proulx 1984:195 leg is honestly marked 'carried' and matches the StressTyp2 passage; (2) Deciding source: a genuine primary reference grammar (Reichard 1925, 215 pp) read in the original, plus a carried comparative sketch (Proulx 1984). It is not the best available description: Teeter 1964 (UCPL 37, 251 pp, Glottolog's top-ranked grammar) has a dedicated treatment of accent phrases/culminative syllable and was not opened by the first reader, the second reader, or me (all open routes blocked: IA lending-only, Google Books 429, eScholarship WAF, HathiTrust 403). Crossref shows no instrumental or later phonological study of Wiyot prosody (language dormant since 1962), so Teeter 1964 is the ceiling. (3) Risk to the classification: low for the lexical-vs-quantity-sensitive que

sources.note: Standard modern reference grammar (last-speaker data) with a phonology section on accent phrases and the culminative syllable (acute/grave); our the primary-stress rule cites Teeter only through Wikipedia. It decides whether the culminative accent is lexically placed per word (lexical stands) or whether a placement rule / phrasal pitch accent analysis is stated, and it can settle StressTyp2's 'leftmost heavy else initial' coding.
